The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of the
imported piecewise $C^1$ boundary and surface-measure definitions
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; let
$E,B$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and $\rho,J$ source fields of
[[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$; and let $(V,\nu_V)$ and $(D,r)$ be the
volume and patch test geometries of [[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]]. Assume the
fields are jointly $C^1$ on $\Omega\times I$ and that the additional
derivatives appearing below exist and are continuous there; for instance $E,B$
jointly of class $C^2$ and $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$ is sufficient.

(a) [Differential implies integral] If the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, then for every
volume test geometry $(V,\nu_V)$ and every $t\in I$,

$$\oint_{\partial V}E(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\int_V\rho(\cdot,t)\,d\lambda_3,\qquad \oint_{\partial V}B(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=0,$$

and for every patch test geometry $(D,r)$ the flux functions
$t\mapsto\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ and
$t\mapsto\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ are differentiable on $I$ and, for
every $t\in I$,

$$\oint_{\partial S}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS,\qquad \oint_{\partial S}B(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=\mu_0\int_SJ(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS+c^{-2}\frac{d}{dt}\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS.$$

(b) [Integral implies differential] Conversely, suppose the two volume
identities of (a) hold for every volume test geometry and every $t\in I$, and
that for every patch test geometry the two flux functions are differentiable
on $I$ and the two patch identities of (a) hold for every $t\in I$. Then the
four smooth-branch equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] hold pointwise on
$\Omega\times I$:

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

The equivalence is asserted for the exact class of test geometries of
[[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]], which contains the open interiors of all closed
axis-parallel boxes compactly contained in $\Omega$ and the affine square
patches; it is not a recovery from one selected volume or one selected patch,
and the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the time derivative of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] are the operators used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention
already carried by the imported finite piecewise $C^1$ boundary presentations
and by the compact $C^1$ surface measure cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ open and
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open interval. This definition fixes the
time-independent spatial test geometries of the integral form of the Maxwell
equations.

(a) [Volume test geometry] A **volume test geometry** in $\Omega$ is a pair
$(V,\nu_V)$ where $V\subseteq\Omega$ is a nonempty bounded open set with
$\overline V\subseteq\Omega$ and a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation
of its boundary ([[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]), and
$\nu_V$ is the outward unit normal of that presentation off its edge set
([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]). The
**closed-surface flux** of a field $F$ continuous on a neighbourhood of
$\overline V$ is the finite face sum

$$\oint_{\partial V}F\cdot\nu_V\,dS:=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_V\,dS,$$

with the face surface integrals of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. For every closed
axis-parallel box $K=\prod_{i<3}[a_i,b_i]\subseteq\Omega$ with $a_i<b_i$, its
open interior $V=\prod_{i<3}(a_i,b_i)$ is a volume test geometry and
$\overline V=K$; its natural six-face presentation is the boundary of $K$, with
outward normals $\pm e_i$. The volume variable is $V$, while $K$ denotes its
compact closure. Each face is a degenerate three-dimensional box and hence has
$\lambda_3$-measure zero by
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]; their finite union
$K\setminus V$ is null. Thus for continuous $h$ on a neighbourhood of $K$,
$\int_Vh\,d\lambda_3=\int_Kh\,d\lambda_3$: the positive and negative integrals
over the null difference vanish by
[[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]] and
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

(b) [Patch test geometry] A **patch test geometry** in $\Omega$ is a regular
$C^2$ surface patch $(D,r)$ over a finite elementary Green region in the sense
of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]
([[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]],
[[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]]): $D\subseteq\mathbb
R^2$ is a finite elementary Green region, $r$ is of class $C^2$ on an open
neighbourhood of $D$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]),
$r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on the interior of $D$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]) and
no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of $D$. Its
**induced boundary chain** $\partial S=r(\partial D)$ and its **circulation**
$\oint_{\partial S}F\cdot d\mathbf r$ for a field continuous on the image are
those of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]
([[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]); its
**oriented flux** of a field $F$ continuous on the image is

$$\int_SF\cdot n_S\,dS:=\int_D(F\circ r)\cdot(r_u\times r_v)\,dudv,$$

the scalar Riemann integral of the continuous integrand on the compact Jordan
parameter region, in the orientation induced by $r$
([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]). The pair $(D,r)$
is part of the data. Every affine graph patch $r(u,v)=(u,v,\varphi(u,v))$ over
an axis-parallel square $D=[c_1,c_1+\ell]\times[c_2,c_2+\ell]$ with $\ell>0$,
whose graph lies in $\Omega$ with $\varphi$ affine (for instance constant), and
more generally every affine regular patch over such a square, is a patch test
geometry: the square is a finite elementary Green region, and $r$ is smooth and
regular with $\varphi_u,\varphi_v$ constant.

(c) [Regularity convention] When an integral identity of this framework is
asserted for a volume test geometry $V$, respectively for a patch test geometry
$S$, with respect to a field $F$ of stated class $C^k$, it concerns fields
defined and of class $C^k$ on an open neighbourhood of $\overline V$ in
$\Omega$, respectively of the image $r[D]$ in $\Omega$; when the identity
involves a time derivative of a flux, the field is defined with the stated
regularity on a neighbourhood of that compact set times the compact time
interval of the assertion. No regularity away from these neighbourhoods is
asserted.

(d) [Conventions and scope] Test geometries are fixed spatial subsets of
$\Omega$ and carry no motion. A patch's orientation is the one induced by its
parametrization, and its induced boundary chain has the compatible orientation
of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]], so that the
classical Stokes theorem applies with a plus sign. The definition retains the
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the imported boundary and surface-measure
definitions; it asserts no differential equation, no physical law and no
existence of fields.

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ with $\omega=c|k|$, let
$e\in\mathbb C^3$ with $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$, and let $(E,B)$ be
the corresponding plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Let $u$ and
$S$ be the energy density and Poynting vector of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and $g=S/c^2$, $\sigma$, $\Pi=-\sigma$ the
momentum density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Write $T=2\pi/\omega$,
$|e|^2=e\cdot\overline e$, $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle f\rangle:=\frac1T\int_0^Tf(x,s)\,ds$ be the period average at fixed
$x$. Then, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$:

(a) [Averaged energy density] $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$,
independent of $x$ and of the starting time.

(b) [Averaged Poynting vector]
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2\hat k$; hence
$\langle S\rangle=\langle u\rangle c\hat k$, and the period-averaged intensity
is $I:=|\langle S\rangle|=c\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2$.

(c) [Averaged momentum density, stress and momentum flux]
$\langle g\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2c}|e|^2\hat k$, and componentwise
$\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$, equivalently
$\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$; the period-averaged
momentum flux across a plane with unit normal $n$ is therefore
$\langle u\rangle(\hat k\cdot n)\hat k$, a pure flux along $\hat k$ with signed
coefficient $(I/c)(\hat k\cdot n)$ and magnitude $(I/c)|\hat k\cdot n|$. The
tensor identity holds for every complex transverse amplitude $e$, not only for
real or circular ones.

(d) [Balance reading] On the source-free region the local identities of
[[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]] hold for this
field; since $u,g,S,\sigma$ are $T$-periodic in $t$, the period averages of
their time derivatives vanish ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]), so averaging the
identities gives $\operatorname{div}\langle S\rangle=0$ and
$\operatorname{div}\langle\sigma\rangle=0$ consistently (both averaged fields
are in fact constant), and the reading of $u,S,g,\Pi$ as energy and momentum
densities and fluxes is that of those two theorems.

(e) [Scope] These are exact identities for the ideal plane wave; $I$ is the
intensity used by the radiation-pressure thought experiment of the companion
page and in radiation-flux arguments. No detection statistics, no finite-beam
or finite-time realisation and no empirical claim is made, and the zero
amplitude gives the zero wave and zero total energy, whereas every nonzero
amplitude gives infinite total energy over $\mathbb R^3$.

Adopt the laboratory region with its inertial chart and fixed-time reading of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]], the electric and magnetic fields of [[def-em-fields]],
the charge parameter, frame charge and current densities and charge integrals
of [[def-em-sources]], and the SI units and constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]. This definition fixes the framework's report-record
vocabulary; it selects no experiment, records no value, evaluates no indicator
and asserts no measurement.

(a) [Primary source] A *primary source* is a declared bibliographic
identification of a report (author, title, date, publication, and the
identification of the passages actually inspected) together with the declared
limits of the reading: which parts of the report were read, which were not, and
any carrier defects (for instance corrupted optical-character-recognition text
of formulae or tables).

(b) [Comparison quantity and measurand] Let $d\ge1$ be an integer. A
*comparison quantity* of dimension $d$ is a declared map from a declared
condition set to $\mathbb R^d$, with declared units, whose components are
finite expressions in specified framework quantities. These may include the
values of $E,B,\rho,J$ at declared events, the charge parameter $q$, and the
declared charge or current integrals of [[def-em-sources]]; declared field
circulations and surface fluxes on the admitted fixed geometries of
[[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]]; and declared finite-time or period averages of
specified derived field quantities, including $u$ and $S$ of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]. An integral or average is admitted only with its
domain, orientation where needed, integration convention and actual
well-definedness hypotheses declared. For example, a component $Q(t)$
continuous on a declared compact interval $[a,b]$ inside the laboratory time
domain, with $a<b$, has the finite Riemann average
$(b-a)^{-1}\int_a^b Q(t)\,dt$ by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]; a
period average additionally declares the period and interval. Field fluxes
inherit the regularity, compactness, boundary presentation and measure/choice
conventions of their fixed-test supplier. A declared detector-response
integral may be used only when its declared model and integral suppliers
establish a finite real value. An extended nonnegative integral with value
$+\infty$ is not a component of this real-valued comparison map or a recorded
finite rate. No existence or finiteness of an arbitrary field integral,
distributional product or detector response is asserted. A *measurand* is a
comparison quantity together with a declared condition description under which
it is to be read. All quantities carry the SI conventions of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(c) [Apparatus and preparation description] An *apparatus-and-preparation
description* is a declared finite record of the apparatus, the preparation,
the controls and the environment in the report's own terms, with the
identification of the passage of the primary source of (a) from which each
item of the description is taken. The definition asserts only that the
description is declared and finite; it asserts nothing about its correctness
or completeness.

(d) [Recorded data and reported observations] For an integer $d\ge1$, a
*recorded datum* is a vector $z_k\in\mathbb R^{d}$ with declared units
together with a *condition annotation* $a_k$, a declared finite text
identifying the declared run condition of the datum and, when the datum is
taken from a report, its locator in the primary source. A *reported
observation* is a declared finite text recording a qualitative observation of
the report. A *record* is a finite tuple of recorded data and reported
observations together with the declared condition annotations. The record
contains no probability space, random variable, distribution, sampling law,
independence assumption, likelihood or coverage statement.

(e) [Calibration model] A *calibration model* is a tuple $(Z,c,\delta)$ in
which $Z$ is a declared nonempty set of *apparatus-output values*,
$c:Z\to\mathbb R^d$ is a declared *calibration map* and
$\delta\in[0,\infty)$ is a declared *calibration-error bound*: it declares
that for every output $o\in Z$ obtained under the declared conditions, the
value of the comparison quantity of (b) lies in the closed box
$\prod_{j=1}^d[c_j(o)-\delta,\,c_j(o)+\delta]$ in the declared units. A
calibration model is a declaration; the definition asserts no accuracy beyond
the bound $\delta$ and no statistical property of $c$ or $\delta$. A declared
*missing* calibration is recorded as missing, and no value or bound is then
available from this clause.

(f) [Uncertainty record] An *uncertainty record* is a finite tuple of declared
bounds, each carrying a declared *source label* from the finite list
$\{calibration,\ resolution,\ systematic,\ sampling-variability,\ rounding,\ other\}$
and a declared value in the declared units; each entry is a declared
constraint of the form of (e), and the record may state that a bound is
unavailable. No entry is a standard-deviation convention, a coverage
probability, a confidence level, a $p$-value, a posterior or a probability
law.

(g) [Analysis assumptions] An *analysis-assumption list* is a finite tuple of
declared assumptions used to obtain the recorded data or to compare them with
a model (binning, background model, selection rules, corrections, fitting or
estimation procedure, independence or dependence of entries, and the
treatment of the sources of uncertainty); declared omissions are recorded as
omissions and are not filled in by the definition.

(h) [Interpretation] An *interpretation* is a declared statement that
identifies a specified model prediction and declares the result of comparing
the record with it (support, constraint, failure to distinguish, or no
conclusion), conditional on (a)-(g). The interpretation is part of the report
account and not of the data; it asserts no probability, no significance level
and no truth of any framework, and it records a comparison of a specified
model, not of a whole theory.

(i) [Well-definedness and scope] All components of (a)-(h) are finite tuples,
real numbers, declared maps on declared sets and finite text labels; forming
this finite vocabulary uses no choice principle. Evaluating a comparison
quantity inherits every hypothesis and axiom of its actual suppliers,
including countable choice when the selected fixed-test surface or
Lebesgue-measure interface requires it; no measurability, integrability,
completeness or differentiability is inferred merely from the record. A
comparison quantity is evaluated only where the cited items supply its
ingredients and a finite value. Missing source detail stays missing: no
universal sampling law, precision, independence, coverage or calibration
correctness is part of the definition, and none may be inferred from it. The
definition is the framework-local vocabulary for the reports of this page; it
does not assert that any laboratory realises a measurand or that any reported
observation is correct.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $\theta_0\in U$, and let $u\in\mathbb R^n$ satisfy $\lVert u\rVert_2=1$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval with $0\in I$ and such that $\gamma(\theta):=\theta_0+\theta u\in U$ for every $\theta\in I$. Let $F:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $F(\theta_0)=0$, and suppose that for every $\theta\in I$ the directional derivative of $F$ along $u$ satisfies

$$D_uF(\theta_0+\theta u)=\langle\nabla F(\theta_0+\theta u),u\rangle\ge m>0$$

([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). Let a recorded scalar $\hat y\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\hat y|\le s$ with $s\ge0$, and let a calibration-error bound $|y-\hat y|\le\delta$ with $\delta\ge0$ hold for $y:=F(\theta_0+\theta u)$ at a candidate $\theta\in I$. Then

$$|\theta|\le\frac{s+\delta}{m},$$

and the corresponding configuration displacement $\gamma(\theta)-\theta_0=\theta u$ has Euclidean length $\lVert\theta u\rVert_2=|\theta|$. The conclusion is a deterministic conditional statement about the stated bounds; it is not a sampling law, a statistical inference, or a claim about any historical report, and the parameters $s,\delta,m$ are supplied by the user of the statement rather than estimated from data here.

[Static branch] Fix the volume test geometry $(V,
u_V)$ and the time $t\in I_t$ of the statement, with $ho(\cdot,t)$ vanishing identically on $V$; under the smooth-branch regularity hypotheses of [F2], clause (a) of [F2] gives $\oint_{\partial V}E(\cdot,t)\cdot
u_V\,dS= rac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\int_Vho(\cdot,t)\,d\lambda_3$, and the integrand $ho(\cdot,t)$ is the identically zero function on $V$, so its integral is $0$ and the flux vanishes: $\oint_{\partial V}E(\cdot,t)\cdot
u_V\,dS=0$, the exact framework prediction for the enclosed-flux observable being $y_0=0$; the test-geometry conventions are those of [F3], and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used here exactly through [F2].

[Wave branch] Let $(E,B)$ be the plane-wave solution with data $(k,\omega,e)$ and let $n$ be a unit vector; clause (b) of [F4] gives the signed identity $\langle S\rangle\cdot n=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2(\hat k\cdot n)$, so if the declared dictionary fixes the comparison quantity as the magnitude $|\langle S\rangle\cdot n|$ of the normal period-averaged flux, the exact framework prediction is $y_0=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2|\hat k\cdot n|$, the absolute value being the declared magnitude convention and not a consequence of the signed identity.

[Displacement interval] Put $J_\theta:=\{\,h\in\mathbb R:\theta_0+h\in I_\theta\,\}$, the translate $I_\theta-\theta_0$ of the nonempty open interval $I_\theta$: $J_\theta$ is a nonempty open interval and contains $0$ because $\theta_0\in I_\theta$, and $f'(\theta_0+h)\ge m>0$ for every $h\in J_\theta$ by the hypothesis $f'\ge m$ on $I_\theta$.

[Conditional confinement] Apply [F6] with $n=1$, $U:=I_\theta$, base point $\theta_0$, unit direction $u:=1\in\mathbb R^1$ (so $\lVert u\rVert_2=1$), interval $I:=J_\theta$ and $F:=f$: $U=I_\theta$ is open and contains $\theta_0$; for every $h\in J_\theta$ one has $\gamma(h)=\theta_0+h\cdot1=\theta_0+h\in I_\theta=U$ by the definition of $J_\theta$; $f$ is of class $C^1$ on $U$ with $f(\theta_0)=0$; and the directional derivative of $f$ along $u=1$ is the ordinary derivative, $D_1f(\theta_0+h)=f'(\theta_0+h)\ge m>0$, because in $\mathbb R^1$ the difference quotient defining $D_1f$ is the ordinary difference quotient. Hence, for every candidate $h\in J_\theta$ for which the record declares $y=f(\theta_0+h)$ with $|\hat y|\le s$ and $|y-\hat y|\le\delta$, [F6] yields $|h|\le(s+\delta)/m$; writing $\theta:=\theta_0+h\in I_\theta$ for the candidate parameter value of the record's declared dictionary, this is exactly $|\theta-\theta_0|\le(s+\delta)/m$, which is clause (b).

[Status] Clause (c) records the scope of steps 1.1-2.1: the result is conditional on the declared family, dictionary, calibration and recorded bounds and on the margin $m$; it is not a sampling law, likelihood, confidence level, coverage probability or $p$-value, and asserts no rejection error rate; the record vocabulary of [F5] supplies only declared comparison quantities, calibration models and analysis assumptions, so the dictionary identification in step 2.1 is a declaration rather than a consequence of the record structure; a discrepancy may lie in the family, the dictionary, the calibration or the analysis, so neither agreement nor disagreement proves or deductively falsifies the framework; the three primary reports recorded on this page supply no calibrated response transfer function, trial-level dataset or sampling law in their recorded read extents, so no numerical bound and no numerical application is asserted for them; and the empirical support relations are nonlogical.

Let $\omega>0$ and let $k_1,k_2\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy
$|k_1|=|k_2|=\omega/c$. For $j=1,2$ let $e_j\in\mathbb C^3$ with
$k_j\cdot e_j=0$, put $b_j=k_j\times e_j/\omega$ and let $(E_j,B_j)$ be the
plane-wave solutions of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] given by
[[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]. Let $a_1,a_2\in\mathbb R$ and put
$(E,B):=a_1(E_1,B_1)+a_2(E_2,B_2)$. Then:

(a) [Superposition] $(E,B)$ is a smooth source-free solution of the vacuum
Maxwell equations ([[pthm-em-linear-superposition]]), and at each fixed $x$ it
can be written with a single phase,
$$E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\alpha(x)\,e^{i(k_1\cdot x-\omega t)}),\qquad B(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\beta(x)\,e^{i(k_1\cdot x-\omega t)}),$$
where $\alpha(x):=a_1e_1+a_2e_2e^{i\delta(x)}$,
$\beta(x):=a_1b_1+a_2b_2e^{i\delta(x)}$ and
$\delta(x):=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x$; constant relative phases are absorbed in $e_2$.

(b) [Averaged energy density with the coherent cross term] For every $x$,
$$\langle u\rangle(x)=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|\alpha(x)|^2+\frac{1}{4\mu_0}|\beta(x)|^2=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\bigl(a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2\bigr)+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(W(x)\bigr),$$
where
$W(x):=\bigl(e_1\cdot\overline e_2+(\hat k_1\times e_1)\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline e_2)\bigr)e^{-i\delta(x)}$.
The first two terms are the sum of the averaged energy densities of the two
waves ([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]]); the third is the interference cross
term, which for a fixed relative phase does not average away.

(c) [Averaged flux and momentum; equal wavevectors] (with $u$ the energy
density and $S$ the Poynting vector of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]])
$\langle S\rangle(x)=\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\alpha(x)\times\overline{\beta(x)}\bigr)$.
In particular, if $k_1=k_2=:k$ then the superposition is the single plane wave
with amplitude $a_1e_1+a_2e_2$, and
$\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|a_1e_1+a_2e_2|^2$,
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|a_1e_1+a_2e_2|^2\hat k$
([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]]).

(d) [No incoherent or statistical claim] The formulas are deterministic
identities for the specified coherent superposition; they are not an ensemble
average over phases, and no detection statistics, finite-sample visibility
estimate or empirical conclusion is drawn. The computation is a conditional
consequence of the adopted Maxwell postulate and does not by itself distinguish
classical from quantum descriptions of light.

Let $\omega>0$ and let $k_1,k_2\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy
$|k_1|=|k_2|=\omega/c$. For $j=1,2$ let $e_j\in\mathbb C^3$ with
$k_j\cdot e_j=0$, put $b_j=k_j\times e_j/\omega$ and let $(E_j,B_j)$ be the
plane-wave solutions of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] given by
[[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]. Let $a_1,a_2\in\mathbb R$ and put
$(E,B):=a_1(E_1,B_1)+a_2(E_2,B_2)$. Then:

(a) [Superposition] $(E,B)$ is a smooth source-free solution of the vacuum
Maxwell equations ([[pthm-em-linear-superposition]]), and at each fixed $x$ it
can be written with a single phase,
$$E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\alpha(x)\,e^{i(k_1\cdot x-\omega t)}),\qquad B(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\beta(x)\,e^{i(k_1\cdot x-\omega t)}),$$
where $\alpha(x):=a_1e_1+a_2e_2e^{i\delta(x)}$,
$\beta(x):=a_1b_1+a_2b_2e^{i\delta(x)}$ and
$\delta(x):=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x$; constant relative phases are absorbed in $e_2$.

(b) [Averaged energy density with the coherent cross term] For every $x$,
$$\langle u\rangle(x)=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|\alpha(x)|^2+\frac{1}{4\mu_0}|\beta(x)|^2=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\bigl(a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2\bigr)+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(W(x)\bigr),$$
where
$W(x):=\bigl(e_1\cdot\overline e_2+(\hat k_1\times e_1)\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline e_2)\bigr)e^{-i\delta(x)}$.
The first two terms are the sum of the averaged energy densities of the two
waves ([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]]); the third is the interference cross
term, which for a fixed relative phase does not average away.

(c) [Averaged flux and momentum; equal wavevectors] (with $u$ the energy
density and $S$ the Poynting vector of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]])
$\langle S\rangle(x)=\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\alpha(x)\times\overline{\beta(x)}\bigr)$.
In particular, if $k_1=k_2=:k$ then the superposition is the single plane wave
with amplitude $a_1e_1+a_2e_2$, and
$\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|a_1e_1+a_2e_2|^2$,
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|a_1e_1+a_2e_2|^2\hat k$
([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]]).

(d) [No incoherent or statistical claim] The formulas are deterministic
identities for the specified coherent superposition; they are not an ensemble
average over phases, and no detection statistics, finite-sample visibility
estimate or empirical conclusion is drawn. The computation is a conditional
consequence of the adopted Maxwell postulate and does not by itself distinguish
classical from quantum descriptions of light.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.
If $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is complex differentiable at $a\in U$, then $f$ is continuous at $a$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$. Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$. Scalar multiples are included among the finite componentwise operations. The assertions remain valid on an empty open domain.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

The relation of [[def-real-order]] is well defined and makes $\mathbb{R}$
([[thm-reals-field]]) a totally ordered field.

Adopt the laboratory region with its inertial chart and fixed-time reading of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]], the electric and magnetic fields of [[def-em-fields]],
the charge parameter, frame charge and current densities and charge integrals
of [[def-em-sources]], and the SI units and constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]. This definition fixes the framework's report-record
vocabulary; it selects no experiment, records no value, evaluates no indicator
and asserts no measurement.

(a) [Primary source] A *primary source* is a declared bibliographic
identification of a report (author, title, date, publication, and the
identification of the passages actually inspected) together with the declared
limits of the reading: which parts of the report were read, which were not, and
any carrier defects (for instance corrupted optical-character-recognition text
of formulae or tables).

(b) [Comparison quantity and measurand] Let $d\ge1$ be an integer. A
*comparison quantity* of dimension $d$ is a declared map from a declared
condition set to $\mathbb R^d$, with declared units, whose components are
finite expressions in specified framework quantities. These may include the
values of $E,B,\rho,J$ at declared events, the charge parameter $q$, and the
declared charge or current integrals of [[def-em-sources]]; declared field
circulations and surface fluxes on the admitted fixed geometries of
[[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]]; and declared finite-time or period averages of
specified derived field quantities, including $u$ and $S$ of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]. An integral or average is admitted only with its
domain, orientation where needed, integration convention and actual
well-definedness hypotheses declared. For example, a component $Q(t)$
continuous on a declared compact interval $[a,b]$ inside the laboratory time
domain, with $a<b$, has the finite Riemann average
$(b-a)^{-1}\int_a^b Q(t)\,dt$ by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]; a
period average additionally declares the period and interval. Field fluxes
inherit the regularity, compactness, boundary presentation and measure/choice
conventions of their fixed-test supplier. A declared detector-response
integral may be used only when its declared model and integral suppliers
establish a finite real value. An extended nonnegative integral with value
$+\infty$ is not a component of this real-valued comparison map or a recorded
finite rate. No existence or finiteness of an arbitrary field integral,
distributional product or detector response is asserted. A *measurand* is a
comparison quantity together with a declared condition description under which
it is to be read. All quantities carry the SI conventions of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(c) [Apparatus and preparation description] An *apparatus-and-preparation
description* is a declared finite record of the apparatus, the preparation,
the controls and the environment in the report's own terms, with the
identification of the passage of the primary source of (a) from which each
item of the description is taken. The definition asserts only that the
description is declared and finite; it asserts nothing about its correctness
or completeness.

(d) [Recorded data and reported observations] For an integer $d\ge1$, a
*recorded datum* is a vector $z_k\in\mathbb R^{d}$ with declared units
together with a *condition annotation* $a_k$, a declared finite text
identifying the declared run condition of the datum and, when the datum is
taken from a report, its locator in the primary source. A *reported
observation* is a declared finite text recording a qualitative observation of
the report. A *record* is a finite tuple of recorded data and reported
observations together with the declared condition annotations. The record
contains no probability space, random variable, distribution, sampling law,
independence assumption, likelihood or coverage statement.

(e) [Calibration model] A *calibration model* is a tuple $(Z,c,\delta)$ in
which $Z$ is a declared nonempty set of *apparatus-output values*,
$c:Z\to\mathbb R^d$ is a declared *calibration map* and
$\delta\in[0,\infty)$ is a declared *calibration-error bound*: it declares
that for every output $o\in Z$ obtained under the declared conditions, the
value of the comparison quantity of (b) lies in the closed box
$\prod_{j=1}^d[c_j(o)-\delta,\,c_j(o)+\delta]$ in the declared units. A
calibration model is a declaration; the definition asserts no accuracy beyond
the bound $\delta$ and no statistical property of $c$ or $\delta$. A declared
*missing* calibration is recorded as missing, and no value or bound is then
available from this clause.

(f) [Uncertainty record] An *uncertainty record* is a finite tuple of declared
bounds, each carrying a declared *source label* from the finite list
$\{calibration,\ resolution,\ systematic,\ sampling-variability,\ rounding,\ other\}$
and a declared value in the declared units; each entry is a declared
constraint of the form of (e), and the record may state that a bound is
unavailable. No entry is a standard-deviation convention, a coverage
probability, a confidence level, a $p$-value, a posterior or a probability
law.

(g) [Analysis assumptions] An *analysis-assumption list* is a finite tuple of
declared assumptions used to obtain the recorded data or to compare them with
a model (binning, background model, selection rules, corrections, fitting or
estimation procedure, independence or dependence of entries, and the
treatment of the sources of uncertainty); declared omissions are recorded as
omissions and are not filled in by the definition.

(h) [Interpretation] An *interpretation* is a declared statement that
identifies a specified model prediction and declares the result of comparing
the record with it (support, constraint, failure to distinguish, or no
conclusion), conditional on (a)-(g). The interpretation is part of the report
account and not of the data; it asserts no probability, no significance level
and no truth of any framework, and it records a comparison of a specified
model, not of a whole theory.

(i) [Well-definedness and scope] All components of (a)-(h) are finite tuples,
real numbers, declared maps on declared sets and finite text labels; forming
this finite vocabulary uses no choice principle. Evaluating a comparison
quantity inherits every hypothesis and axiom of its actual suppliers,
including countable choice when the selected fixed-test surface or
Lebesgue-measure interface requires it; no measurability, integrability,
completeness or differentiability is inferred merely from the record. A
comparison quantity is evaluated only where the cited items supply its
ingredients and a finite value. Missing source detail stays missing: no
universal sampling law, precision, independence, coverage or calibration
correctness is part of the definition, and none may be inferred from it. The
definition is the framework-local vocabulary for the reports of this page; it
does not assert that any laboratory realises a measurand or that any reported
observation is correct.

derivations.claim: Since $\delta(x_0)\equiv\pi\pmod{2\pi}$, there is an integer $n$ with $\delta(x_0)=\pi+2\pi n$; the cartesian form of [F6] gives $e^{i\delta(x_0)}=\cos\delta(x_0)+i\sin\delta(x_0)$, and [F7] gives $\cos(y+2\pi)=-\cos(y+\pi)=\cos y$ and $\sin(y+2\pi)=-\sin(y+\pi)=\sin y$ for every real $y$, so by induction on $|n|$ one has $\cos(\pi+2\pi n)=\cos\pi=-1$ and $\sin(\pi+2\pi n)=\sin\pi=0$; hence $e^{i\delta(x_0)}=-1$.

[Regularity of $\alpha$] The phase $x\mapsto\delta(x)=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x$ is an affine map $\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$, hence of class $C^\infty$; the exponential is entire [F19], hence complex differentiable everywhere and continuous [F20]; by the algebra-and-composition closure of [F21] the composite $x\mapsto e^{i\delta(x)}$ and the finite combinations defining the components of $\alpha=a_1e_1+a_2e_2e^{i\delta(x)}$ of [F1] are continuous, and the modulus squared $|\alpha|^2=\alpha\cdot\overline\alpha$ [F5] is a finite sum of products of continuous real functions, hence continuous on $\mathbb R^3$.

[Constant background] For a constant $b=b_0>0$ the zero extension is the nonnegative simple function $\tilde b=b_0\chi_W$ with $W\in\mathcal L(\mathbb R^3)$ [F10, F11]; its simple integral is $b_0\lambda_3(W)$ by [F17] and equals its Lebesgue integral by [F18], so $\int_W b\,d\lambda_3=b_0\lambda_3(W)$ by [F14], a value in $(0,+\infty]$ that may be $+\infty$ when $\lambda_3(W)=+\infty$.

[Zero response coefficient] For $\kappa=0$ the field contribution is the zero function because $|\alpha|^2$ is real-valued, so no product $0\cdot(+\infty)$ is formed; then $\int_W\kappa|\alpha|^2\,d\lambda_3=0$ by the $c=0$ clause of [F16], and $R(W)=\int_W b\,d\lambda_3$; in particular the response remains defined in $[0,+\infty]$ on every measurable bin.
Substituting the amplitude data of [F1] and step 1.1 gives $\alpha(x_0)=a_1e_1+a_2e_2e^{i\delta(x_0)}=ae\,(1+(-1))=0$, using $a_1=a_2=a$ and $e_1=e_2=e$.

For $\beta(x_0)$: substituting $a_1=a_2=a$, $e_1=e_2=e$ and step 1.1 into [F1] gives $\beta(x_0)=a(b_1-b_2)$, and $b_1-b_2=k_1\times e/\omega-k_2\times e/\omega=\bigl((k_1-k_2)\times e\bigr)/\omega$ by the coordinate bilinearity of [F3]; if $\beta(x_0)=0$ then multiplying by the nonzero scalar $\omega/a$ (nonzero because $a>0$ and $\omega>0$ from [F1]) gives $(k_1-k_2)\times e=-(k_2-k_1)\times e=0$ by [F3], contrary to the hypothesis $(k_2-k_1)\times e\ne0$; hence $\beta(x_0)\ne0$.

[Integrand measurability and the response functional] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ the family $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^3)$ is a sigma-algebra and $\lambda_3$ a measure on it [F11], and the bin $W$ is measurable with $\lambda_3(W)$ defined [F10]; $|\alpha|^2$ is continuous by step 1.2, hence Borel measurable [F12] and Lebesgue measurable [F13]; since $\kappa\in\mathbb R$, the scaled function $\kappa|\alpha|^2$ is measurable by [F15], and the sum $\kappa|\alpha|^2+\tilde b$ is measurable by [F15] because $\tilde b$ is real-valued and measurable by the declared detector model; consequently [F14] defines $R(W):=\int_W(\kappa|\alpha|^2+b)\,d\lambda_3=\int(\kappa|\alpha|^2+\tilde b)\chi_W\,d\lambda_3\in[0,+\infty]$.

[Finite-rate branch] Suppose $0<\lambda_3(W)<\infty$ and $0<b_0<\infty$. For every $x$ one has $|e^{i\delta(x)}|=1$ by [F6], so $|1+e^{i\delta(x)}|\le1+|e^{i\delta(x)}|=2$ by the triangle inequality of [F5], and $|\alpha(x)|=|a|\,|e|\,|1+e^{i\delta(x)}|\le2a|e|$ by the multiplicative law of [F5], where $|e|^2=\langle e,e\rangle$ is the Euclidean squared norm of the real amplitude [F4]; hence $|\alpha|^2\le4a^2|e|^2$ and, since $\kappa\ge0$, the pointwise bounds $b_0\chi_W\le(\kappa|\alpha|^2+b_0)\chi_W\le C\chi_W$ hold with the finite real constant $C:=4\kappa a^2|e|^2+b_0$. Monotonicity and the simple-integral values of step 1.3 and [F17], [F18] give $0<b_0\lambda_3(W)\le R(W)\le C\lambda_3(W)<\infty$, the strict lower bound by the sign rule $b_0\lambda_3(W)>0$ of [F22] applied to $b_0>0$ and $\lambda_3(W)>0$; thus on this branch $R(W)$ is a finite positive rate.

By clause (a) of [F1], $E(x_0,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\alpha(x_0)\,e^{i(k_1\cdot x_0-\omega t)}\bigr)=\operatorname{Re}(0)=0$ for every real $t$; hence the electric field of the superposition vanishes at $x_0$ at every time, and with step 2.1 the electric term $\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|\alpha(x_0)|^2$ of the averaged density of [F2] vanishes there.

[F2] and step 2.1 give $\langle u\rangle(x_0)=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|\alpha(x_0)|^2+\frac{1}{4\mu_0}|\beta(x_0)|^2=\frac{1}{4\mu_0}|\beta(x_0)|^2$; since $\beta(x_0)\ne0$ by step 2.2, positive definiteness [F4] and the modulus law $|z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0$ of [F5] give $|\beta(x_0)|^2>0$, and $\mu_0>0$ from [F8] gives $1/(4\mu_0)>0$, so the sign rules [F22] yield $\langle u\rangle(x_0)>0$; thus the full averaged energy density does not vanish at $x_0$, only its electric term does.

[General background lower bound] The functions $\tilde b$ and $\kappa|\alpha|^2+\tilde b$ are measurable, nonnegative and finite-valued, with $\tilde b\le\kappa|\alpha|^2+\tilde b$ pointwise because $|\alpha|^2\ge0$ [F5] and $\kappa\ge0$; the monotonicity clause of [F16] and $R(W)=\int(\kappa|\alpha|^2+\tilde b)\chi_W\,d\lambda_3$ of step 2.3 give $\int_W b\,d\lambda_3=\int\tilde b\chi_W\,d\lambda_3\le R(W)$, so $\int_W b\,d\lambda_3>0$ implies $R(W)\ge\int_W b\,d\lambda_3>0$ even though $|\alpha(x_0)|^2=0$ by step 2.1.

[Record versus prediction] The data of [F23] are finite tuples of recorded values or reported observations with declared conditions, calibration and uncertainty, and contain no sampling law; the predictions of steps 1.1-3.3 are deterministic field quantities or a declared extended response functional with a finite real rate only on the branch of step 2.4; a detection and a finite record are different objects from the ideal intensity, so no sampling law, probability of failing a visibility criterion, detection statistics or measured histogram is asserted here, and the finite positive bin prediction of step 2.4 is compatible with the pointwise ideal zero of steps 2.1 and 3.1 without discriminating the classical and quantum descriptions of light, since classical electromagnetic waves interfere.

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], so
that $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$
is nonempty open, $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ is the position in the spatial chart,
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the frame basis of the spatial slice, and the spatial inner
product is the Euclidean form $\delta$; let the units and the constants $c>0$,
$\mu_0>0$ and $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]; let $k\ge1$, and let
$E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be an electric and a magnetic field of class
$C^k$ of [[def-em-fields]]. Write $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $|\cdot|$ for
the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
$\times$ for the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

(a) [Energy density and flux] The **electromagnetic energy density**
$u:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and the **energy flux density** (the **Poynting
vector**) $S:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are defined by

$$u(x,t):=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\,\langle E(x,t),E(x,t)\rangle+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\,\langle B(x,t),B(x,t)\rangle,\qquad S(x,t):=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\,E(x,t)\times B(x,t).$$

At fixed $t\in I$ the map $u(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is a real-valued
function on $\Omega$ and $S(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is a spatial vector
field on $\Omega$, read in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The energy density
carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and
the energy flux density carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-3}$.

(b) [Regularity] If $E,B$ are of class $C^k$, then $u$ and $S$ are of class
$C^k$: they are the components of a polynomial expression in the components of
$E,B$, and the verification below exhibits the composite map. In particular $u$
and $S$ are continuous, and the definitions use no derivative of the fields.

(c) [Pointwise reading, quadratic character] The definitions use only the values
of $E$ and $B$ at the same point $(x,t)$, and they are quadratic in the fields:
for every real $\lambda$ one has $u(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2u(E,B)$ and
$S(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2S(E,B)$, and $u\ge0$. Consequently
decompositions of the fields do not make $u$ or $S$ additive; cross terms
generally contribute. No convention beyond the fixed laboratory frame enters
the definitions.

(d) [Products and singular support] If $E,B$ are only locally integrable (the
weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]), the products $E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and
the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally integrable, and no product of
distributions is defined. The displayed formulas then define $u$ and $S$
pointwise almost everywhere, and the framework uses them only where the local
integrability of the products, respectively of the component being integrated,
is separately established. No value of $u$ or $S$ is assigned at a point of
singular source support.

(e) [Status] This item defines quantities only. The interpretation of $u$ as an
energy density and of $S$ as an energy flux density, and every balance identity
involving them, is the content of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and of the other
balance items of this page; no identification of $(u,S)$ with components of a
covariant tensor is made here, and the relation $S=c^2g$ to the momentum density
$g$ of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]] is a consequence of those definitions,
not an identification made at this point.

Let $\omega>0$, $k:=\omega/c$ with $c$ the vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]], $\mu_0>0$ the vacuum permeability of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and $p_0\in\mathbb C^3$ (the complex dipole-moment amplitude, in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m$). Define, on the punctured space $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and all times $t\in\mathbb R$,

$$E_{\rm d}(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(-\frac{\mu_0\omega^2}{4\pi r}\,n\times(n\times p_0)\,e^{i(kr-\omega t)}\Bigr),\qquad B_{\rm d}(x,t):=\frac1c\,n\times E_{\rm d}(x,t),$$

where $r:=|x|$ and $n:=x/r$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), with the real part and complex exponential of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] and [[def-complex-exponential]] and the componentwise real-part encoding convention of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] (the spatial amplitude here varies with $x$; no plane-wave instance is asserted). Call $(E_{\rm d},B_{\rm d})$ the **ideal harmonic electric-dipole radiation model of frequency $\omega$ and amplitude $p_0$**, and call $S_{\rm d}:=E_{\rm d}\times B_{\rm d}/\mu_0$ its model flux ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]); the model fields are read as an electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]].

### Adopted status

This is an explicitly adopted ideal radiation-law model, fixed by the following declarations.

1. It is the leading transverse far-zone field of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]](c) evaluated at the harmonic transverse moment $V(u)=\operatorname{Re}(-\omega^2p_0e^{-i\omega u})$, i.e. at $p''$ for the waveform $p(u)=\operatorname{Re}(p_0e^{-i\omega u})$: by part (a) of [[lem-em-harmonic-forcing-periodic-response]] the second derivative of that explicit $C^\infty$ waveform is $\operatorname{Re}(-\omega^2p_0e^{-i\omega u})$, and substituting $u=t-r/c$ into $\mu_0\,n\times(n\times V(u))/(4\pi r)$ gives exactly $E_{\rm d}$, because $e^{i(kr-\omega t)}=e^{-i\omega(t-r/c)}$.
2. The model contains no independent magnetic-dipole or higher-multipole radiation, no near-zone or static field and no other radiating component.
3. It is not asserted to solve the vacuum Maxwell equations at finite $r$, to be the field of any actual source, to satisfy any boundary condition or to have finite total energy on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$.
4. For compact smooth conserved sources, comparison with these prescribed model fields uses the actual source's moment $p_{\rm act}(u)$ of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]], the harmonic waveform $p_{\rm h}(u)=\operatorname{Re}(p_0e^{-i\omega u})$, their second-derivative mismatch

$$M(u):=|p_{\rm act}''(u)-p_{\rm h}''(u)|,$$

and the explicit $D,\Gamma$ bounds of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]] (b), (c) and (e). A bound depending only on that source's $D$ and $\Gamma$ is valid when $M\equiv0$ on the observation window, in which case the theorem's leading fields for the source's moment coincide with the model fields; for $M\not\equiv0$ the comparison carries the additional mismatch term. The source's moment is not automatically the independently prescribed $p_0$. These actual-source comparisons assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) carried by the cited theorem. The explicit ideal fields themselves and their pointwise flux definition remain choice-free.

No measured, empirical or material-response content is adopted: $p_0$ is prescribed model data, not a derived polarizability.

### Well-definedness and conventions

On the declared domain $r>0$, so $r=|x|$ is the positive Euclidean norm and $n=x/r$ is a unit vector; $n\times(n\times p_0)$ and its real part are defined componentwise, and $E_{\rm d}$, $B_{\rm d}$ are $C^\infty$ on $(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb R$ because $r$ is $C^\infty$ there and the real and imaginary parts of $-\frac{\mu_0\omega^2}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times p_0)e^{i(kr-\omega t)}$ are smooth combinations of the smooth functions $r^{-1}$, $x_i$, $\cos(kr-\omega t)$ and $\sin(kr-\omega t)$ ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]). The field is transverse in the sense that $E_{\rm d}\cdot n=0$ and $B_{\rm d}\cdot n=0$, because $n\times(n\times p_0)$ is orthogonal to $n$ and $n\times E_{\rm d}$ is orthogonal to $n$ by [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]] applied separately to real and imaginary parts, and $B_{\rm d}=n\times E_{\rm d}/c$ holds by definition with $|B_{\rm d}|=|E_{\rm d}|/c$. The model is meaningful at $p_0=0$, where both fields and the flux vanish identically. The varying radial amplitude $1/r$ is not a plane-wave amplitude, and the componentwise real-part convention is that of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; the cross product, inner product and norms are those of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. No equation of motion of any source, no determination of $p_0$ from any charge distribution and no energy or flux reading beyond the pointwise definition of $S_{\rm d}$ in [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] is part of this item.

Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular
frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$
the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic
fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be
those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose
convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is
used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$

componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$,
$\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**,
$\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the
**angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**,
and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then:

(a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ in the sense of
[[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; on the whole-space laboratory region
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an
electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class
$C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

(b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is
affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the
$e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through
$\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$.

(c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave
**nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the
magnetic field alone determines $b$, because
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$
(evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$).

(d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It
asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no
energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The
units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is
claimed.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a
real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and
$\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential
series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number
$e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and
$B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$,
$T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map
$(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
as its domain, and the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a) is the one proved in
[[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] for the encoded expressions; the statement of
this definition uses that regularity and adds no further analytic property.
The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of
$w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking
$\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is
immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real
linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are
constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no
matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this
definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the
Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are
defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ and $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, and let
$(E,B)$ be the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on the
whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with the terminology and
phase convention of that definition, the cross product and inner product of
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] extended to
$\mathbb C^3$ componentwise, the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\hat k=k/|k|$. Then:

(a) [Amplitude equations] $(E,B)$ satisfies the four smooth-branch vacuum
Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$ and
$J\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if

$$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot b=0,\qquad k\times e=\omega b,\qquad k\times b=-\frac{\omega}{c^2}e .$$

(b) [Dispersion, nonzero waves, two polarizations] The amplitude equations
admit a nonzero solution $(e,b)\ne(0,0)$ if and only if
$|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$; off this dispersion relation the only solution is
$e=b=0$. On the dispersion relation both zero and nonzero solutions occur; a
particular solution is nonzero exactly when its amplitudes are not both zero,
in the sense of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]](c). If $|k|=\omega/c$, the
solutions are exactly the pairs $(e,b)$ with
$e\in\{v\in\mathbb C^3: k\cdot v=0\}$ arbitrary and $b=k\times e/\omega$: a
complex two-dimensional family; $e=0$ gives the zero wave, and for every
nonzero solution $e\ne0$ and $b\ne0$.

(c) [Transversality, orthogonality, magnitude relation and the wave equation]
For every solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ and every
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: $k\cdot E(x,t)=k\cdot B(x,t)=0$,
$E(x,t)\cdot B(x,t)=0$ and $B(x,t)=\hat k\times E(x,t)/c$; in particular
$|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$. Each component of $E$ and of $B$ is a $C^\infty$
solution of the wave equation $\Delta v=c^{-2}\partial_t^2v$ of
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(d) [Scope] The equivalence in (a) is between the amplitude equations and
membership in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch; it says nothing about
fields that solve the wave equations but not the amplitude equations (see
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]](b)). The item covers ideal whole-space plane
waves only, makes no finite-energy, boundary, material or empirical claim, and
is conditional on the adopted postulate.

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ with $\omega=c|k|$, let
$e\in\mathbb C^3$ with $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$, and let $(E,B)$ be
the corresponding plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Let $u$ and
$S$ be the energy density and Poynting vector of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and $g=S/c^2$, $\sigma$, $\Pi=-\sigma$ the
momentum density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Write $T=2\pi/\omega$,
$|e|^2=e\cdot\overline e$, $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle f\rangle:=\frac1T\int_0^Tf(x,s)\,ds$ be the period average at fixed
$x$. Then, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$:

(a) [Averaged energy density] $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$,
independent of $x$ and of the starting time.

(b) [Averaged Poynting vector]
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2\hat k$; hence
$\langle S\rangle=\langle u\rangle c\hat k$, and the period-averaged intensity
is $I:=|\langle S\rangle|=c\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2$.

(c) [Averaged momentum density, stress and momentum flux]
$\langle g\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2c}|e|^2\hat k$, and componentwise
$\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$, equivalently
$\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$; the period-averaged
momentum flux across a plane with unit normal $n$ is therefore
$\langle u\rangle(\hat k\cdot n)\hat k$, a pure flux along $\hat k$ with signed
coefficient $(I/c)(\hat k\cdot n)$ and magnitude $(I/c)|\hat k\cdot n|$. The
tensor identity holds for every complex transverse amplitude $e$, not only for
real or circular ones.

(d) [Balance reading] On the source-free region the local identities of
[[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]] hold for this
field; since $u,g,S,\sigma$ are $T$-periodic in $t$, the period averages of
their time derivatives vanish ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]), so averaging the
identities gives $\operatorname{div}\langle S\rangle=0$ and
$\operatorname{div}\langle\sigma\rangle=0$ consistently (both averaged fields
are in fact constant), and the reading of $u,S,g,\Pi$ as energy and momentum
densities and fluxes is that of those two theorems.

(e) [Scope] These are exact identities for the ideal plane wave; $I$ is the
intensity used by the radiation-pressure thought experiment of the companion
page and in radiation-flux arguments. No detection statistics, no finite-beam
or finite-time realisation and no empirical claim is made, and the zero
amplitude gives the zero wave and zero total energy, whereas every nonzero
amplitude gives infinite total energy over $\mathbb R^3$.

Let $\omega>0$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega>0$.

**Scalar form.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C$. Then

$$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\overline d\bigr).$$

**Vector forms.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$, write the same symbols for the componentwise complex-bilinear extensions of the Euclidean inner product and of the cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] to $\mathbb C^3$, and let $\operatorname{Re}$ act componentwise. Then

$$\frac1T\int_0^T\bigl\langle\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr),\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\bigr\rangle\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\langle a,\overline d\rangle\bigr),\qquad \frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\times\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\times\overline d\bigr),$$

the integrals of the real vector-valued integrands being componentwise. The real-valued functions $\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})$ are the time-dependent factors of the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] at a fixed position, with the phase absorbed into $a$ and $d$; no electromagnetic interpretation is asserted. Real quadratic expressions may not be replaced by complex quadratic expressions without conjugation: the left-hand side of the scalar identity is not $\frac12\operatorname{Re}(ad\,e^{-2i\omega t})$ in general, and the two expressions differ already at $t=0$ for $a=d=1+i$.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.
